You're going to be very happy about this. I'll send over the confirmation. And listen, when this pops, we'll talk about the next opportunity. I've got a pipeline of these kinds of plays.

conversation.speaker: client
conversation.text: Wait — what are the commissions on this? And do I get any paperwork before the trade goes through?

conversation.speaker: advisor
conversation.text: The commission is standard — it'll be on your confirmation statement. And yes, you'll get all the trade documentation after it settles. Don't worry about the paperwork side, we handle all of that. The important thing is you're in. Congratulations, Mr. Hensley.

conversation.speaker: client
conversation.text: I hope you're right about this, Marcus. I really can't afford to lose ten thousand dollars.

conversation.speaker: advisor
conversation.text: You're not going to lose it. Trust me. I'll check in with you next week, and I think you're going to see some very nice movement. Take care, Mr. Hensley.

legal_assessment.analysis:
This conversation exhibits the hallmarks of a classic boiler room operation, directly paralleling the conduct described in the NASD disciplinary action against Ford and Andrews at Hibbard, Brown & Co. The advisor, Marcus Devlin, employs aggressive high-pressure sales tactics to push a low-priced, speculative security on an unsuitable client. He makes materially misleading statements, including near-guarantees of price appreciation ('this is as close to a sure thing as you'll ever see'), claims of imminent catalytic events based on purported insider knowledge, assertions that he has invested his own family members' money in the stock, and artificial urgency created by claims of limited share availability. These representations, if false or materially misleading, constitute securities fraud under Section 10(b) and Rule 10b-5 of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934.

The suitability violations are equally egregious. Mr. Hensley is a 57-year-old conservative investor nearing retirement, with modest savings predominantly in blue chips and a bond fund. Recommending that such a client concentrate a significant portion of his liquid savings into a single low-priced speculative security is fundamentally unsuitable under FINRA Rule 2111 (and its predecessor, the NASD suitability rule). The advisor actively discouraged the client from taking time to consider the investment, refused to provide research materials, and pressured him into an immediate decision — all tactics characteristic of boiler room operations. The advisor also failed to adequately disclose risks, commissions, or the speculative nature of the security, instead minimizing risk with misleading reassurances.

Additionally, there are significant supervisory concerns under FINRA Rule 3110. The pattern described — recruiting clients through cold calling, using scripted high-pressure tactics, pushing a single speculative low-priced stock, and discouraging client due diligence — suggests a systemic firm-level failure to establish and maintain adequate supervisory procedures. The advisor's conduct also violates FINRA Rule 2010 (Standards of Commercial Honor and Just and Equitable Principles of Trade) by engaging in manipulative, deceptive, and fundamentally dishonest practices in dealing with a public customer.

legal_assessment.recommendation: The advisor should have conducted a thorough suitability analysis before making any recommendation, taking into account the client's age, risk tolerance, investment objectives, time horizon, and financial situation. A low-priced speculative biotech stock is categorically unsuitable for a 57-year-old conservative investor approaching retirement. The advisor should have provided written research materials and a risk disclosure document, given the client adequate time to make an informed decision, clearly disclosed all commissions and fees, avoided making guarantees or near-guarantees of performance, and refrained from creating artificial urgency. The firm should have supervisory systems in place to detect and prevent these aggressive sales patterns. Based on the severity of the conduct — which mirrors the boiler room operations at Hibbard, Brown & Co. that led to bars and suspensions — appropriate sanctions would include a bar from the securities industry, disgorgement of commissions, and potential referral for criminal prosecution if the misrepresentations were knowingly false.

conversation.speaker: client
conversation.text: Hi Marcus, thanks for meeting with me. I've been doing some reading about this Regulation Best Interest thing, and I want to make sure I understand what it means for our relationship.

conversation.speaker: advisor
conversation.text: Of course, Linda. Happy to talk about it. Regulation BI is basically the SEC's way of saying that when I make a recommendation to you, I need to act in your best interest. It went into effect in June 2020.

conversation.speaker: client
conversation.text: Okay, but I thought that was always the case? I mean, aren't you supposed to be looking out for me?

conversation.speaker: advisor
conversation.text: Well, before Reg BI, broker-dealers like our firm operated under what's called a suitability standard. That meant the recommendation just had to be suitable for you — match your general profile. Now, the standard is higher. We have to consider costs, reasonably available alternatives, and disclose conflicts of interest.

conversation.speaker: client
conversation.text: So what's the difference between what you do and what a fiduciary does? My neighbor uses an RIA and she keeps telling me I should switch.

conversation.speaker: advisor
conversation.text: That's a great question. Investment advisers have a fiduciary duty, which is an ongoing obligation to act in your best interest. As a broker-dealer, my obligation under Reg BI kicks in at the point of recommendation. Between those touchpoints, the standard is different. But honestly, Linda, the practical effect is very similar. Don't let anyone tell you you're getting worse service here.

conversation.speaker: client
conversation.text: But is it really similar? I read that some consumer groups think Reg BI doesn't go far enough — that it's not actually a fiduciary standard even though it sounds like one.

conversation.speaker: advisor
conversation.text: Look, there are always critics. The SEC spent years developing this rule. Industry groups, state regulators, consumer advocates — everyone weighed in. The SEC balanced investor protection with investor choice. If they imposed a full fiduciary standard on broker-dealers, a lot of firms would stop serving smaller accounts. You might lose access to the kind of advice you get from me.

conversation.speaker: client
conversation.text: That sounds like an argument for the industry's benefit, not mine. I want to know specifically — when you recommended I put $150,000 into that variable annuity last year, were you acting under this best interest standard?

conversation.speaker: advisor
conversation.text: Absolutely. I evaluated your situation — your age, your risk tolerance, your income needs in retirement — and that product fit your profile. Variable annuities provide guaranteed income, which is important for someone in your situation.

conversation.speaker: client
conversation.text: But Marcus, I later found out the fees on that annuity are almost 3% annually. And you earned a pretty significant commission on it, didn't you? Shouldn't you have told me about cheaper alternatives?

conversation.speaker: advisor
conversation.text: I did disclose that I receive compensation — that's part of the CRS form we gave you. And the fees reflect the insurance guarantees built into the product. A low-cost index fund doesn't give you the same downside protection.

conversation.speaker: client
conversation.text: I went back and looked at that CRS form. It's two pages of very general language. It didn't tell me how much you personally earned from recommending that specific annuity versus, say, a balanced fund. That feels like a pretty important detail.

conversation.speaker: advisor
conversation.text: The Form CRS is designed to be a summary document. We also provided you the annuity prospectus, which details the fees. I understand your frustration, but the disclosures were made in accordance with what the rules require.

conversation.speaker: client
conversation.text: Okay, but here's what bothers me. You said Reg BI requires you to consider reasonably available alternatives. Did you actually compare the annuity to a portfolio of low-cost ETFs with a systematic withdrawal plan? Because from what I can tell, that would have saved me tens of thousands of dollars over the next twenty years.

conversation.speaker: advisor
conversation.text: Linda, I considered your full picture. The annuity provides certainty. Markets go up and down. I can't guarantee what an ETF portfolio would do. I made a recommendation I believed was in your best interest.

conversation.speaker: client
conversation.text: It just feels like the guaranteed income feature was the justification, but the commission was the motivation. I'm not accusing you of anything, but I want to understand — under this Regulation Best Interest, could I challenge this recommendation?

conversation.speaker: advisor
conversation.text: You can always raise concerns. But I want to assure you, I followed the process — disclosure, care, conflict mitigation. That's what Reg BI requires. If you want, I can schedule a full portfolio review and we can revisit the annuity position in the context of your overall plan.

conversation.speaker: client
conversation.text: I think I'd like that. And I'd also like a written explanation of exactly what alternatives you considered and why the annuity was superior. Can you do that?

conversation.speaker: advisor
conversation.text: I can put together a summary of my analysis. That's a reasonable request, and I'm happy to do it.

legal_assessment.analysis:
This conversation raises several concerns under Regulation Best Interest (17 C.F.R. § 240.15l-1), which imposes four component obligations on broker-dealers: a Disclosure Obligation, a Care Obligation, a Conflict of Interest Obligation, and a Compliance Obligation. The advisor's recommendation of a high-cost variable annuity generating significant commission income implicates all four components. Under the Care Obligation, the advisor must exercise reasonable diligence, care, and skill to understand the potential risks, rewards, and costs of the recommendation, and must have a reasonable basis to believe the recommendation is in the customer's best interest and does not place the financial interest of the broker-dealer ahead of the customer's interest. The client's pointed questions about whether lower-cost alternatives were meaningfully evaluated — particularly a systematic withdrawal plan from low-cost ETFs — suggest the advisor may not have conducted the kind of rigorous comparative analysis that Reg BI contemplates. The advisor's justification centers on the 'certainty' of guaranteed income without addressing cost differentials, which is insufficient under the Care Obligation's requirement to consider reasonably available alternatives.

The Disclosure and Conflict of Interest Obligations also appear to be inadequately addressed. The advisor points to the Form CRS and annuity prospectus as sufficient disclosure, but Reg BI requires disclosure of material facts relating to the scope and terms of the relationship, including all material conflicts of interest associated with the recommendation — specifically the compensation differential between the recommended product and alternatives. Generic disclosure in a two-page CRS form does not satisfy the obligation to disclose specific conflicts at the point of recommendation. Furthermore, the Conflict of Interest Obligation requires the firm to establish policies and procedures to identify, disclose, and mitigate — or in some cases eliminate — conflicts of interest. The advisor's deflection of the commission question and reliance on boilerplate disclosures raises questions about whether the firm's conflict mitigation policies are adequate.

Notably, this scenario also touches on the broader policy debate at the heart of the source litigation. The amici brief from SIFMA and others argued that Reg BI appropriately 'balances' investor protection with investor choice, and that imposing a fiduciary standard would reduce access to advice for smaller investors. The advisor echoes this framing almost verbatim when he warns the client about losing access to advice if a fiduciary standard were imposed — an argument that, while policy-relevant, does not excuse the advisor from his existing obligations under the rule as adopted.

Potential failure to satisfy the Disclosure Obligation by relying on generic Form CRS language rather than providing specific point-of-recommendation disclosure of material compensation conflicts
Potential failure to satisfy the Conflict of Interest Obligation by not adequately mitigating the financial incentive created by the annuity commission, which may have influenced the recommendation
Inadequate documentation of the basis for the recommendation and the comparative analysis of alternatives, which undermines the firm's ability to demonstrate compliance

Reg. 33318 (July 12, 2019)
legal_assessment.recommendation: The advisor should have conducted and documented a thorough comparative analysis of reasonably available alternatives — including lower-cost investment options such as diversified ETF portfolios with systematic withdrawal strategies — before recommending the variable annuity. The specific commission earned on the recommended product versus alternatives should have been disclosed to the client at the point of recommendation, not buried in generic form disclosures. The firm should review its conflict of interest policies and procedures to ensure they require meaningful mitigation measures where compensation differentials create incentives to recommend higher-cost products. Going forward, the advisor should provide the client with written documentation of the rationale for the recommendation, including the alternatives considered and reasons they were rejected, to demonstrate compliance with the Care Obligation. If the comparative analysis cannot support the annuity recommendation on its merits independent of the compensation incentive, the firm should consider whether the recommendation should be reversed or modified.

conversation.speaker: advisor
conversation.text: Of course, Helen. I'm always happy to talk about our process. What's on your mind?

conversation.text: Well, I came across this concept of a 'best interest duty' — apparently there's been a big debate in Canada and elsewhere about whether advisers should be legally required to act in their client's best interest. Are you required to act in my best interest?

conversation.speaker: advisor

conversation.speaker: client

conversation.speaker: client
conversation.text: I'd like that very much. But I also want to understand — for the recommendations you've already made, particularly the DSC funds and the heavy allocation to proprietary products — do I have any recourse if those weren't truly in my best interest?

conversation.speaker: advisor

conversation.speaker: client

conversation.speaker: advisor

conversation.speaker: client
conversation.text: That sounds like a good start. And the compensation — the trailing commissions, the internal incentives for proprietary products — I want full transparency on all of that. Not buried in a disclosure document, but actually explained to me before I agree to anything.

conversation.speaker: advisor
conversation.text: Absolutely. I'll prepare a clear breakdown of the compensation I receive on each product in your portfolio, and for any future recommendation, I'll disclose the compensation impact alongside the recommendation. You deserve to know that.

conversation.speaker: client

legal_assessment.analysis:
This conversation reveals several significant regulatory and conduct concerns that span multiple jurisdictions' standards. The adviser, Marcus, initially deflects the client's questions about the applicable standard of conduct, conflating 'suitability' with 'best interest' before eventually acknowledging the distinction. His past recommendations — DSC mutual funds with significantly higher embedded commissions and a heavy allocation to proprietary products with internal sales incentives — represent classic examples of the misaligned incentive structures and conflicts of interest that the CSA identified in Consultation Paper 33-403 as key investor protection concerns. The fact that DSC funds were subsequently banned in Canada retroactively validates the client's concern that 'suitability' was insufficient to protect her from conflicted advice. The adviser's failure to proactively disclose the material difference in commission structures between DSC and front-end load or fee-based fund classes at the point of sale is particularly problematic.

When viewed through the lens of international standards, the adviser's conduct would likely fall short of the UK FCA's Consumer Duty (PRIN 12), which requires firms to act to deliver good outcomes for retail customers and places affirmative obligations regarding price and value, consumer understanding, and consumer support. Under MiFID II Article 25, the concentration of proprietary products without documented consideration of alternatives would raise serious concerns about whether the firm placed its own commercial interests above the client's. IOSCO's 2021 Suitability Principles emphasize that firms should have policies to manage conflicts of interest arising from remuneration and sales incentives, and ASIC's section 961B requires advisers to demonstrate that they acted in the client's best interest by considering a reasonable range of products. The adviser's admission that internal incentives exist to recommend proprietary funds, combined with the apparent lack of documented product comparison, suggests that these international standards were not met.

The adviser's eventual commitment to enhanced transparency and documented best-interest rationale for future recommendations is constructive but does not address the historical conduct issues. The client's outstanding exposure to proprietary products and the historical DSC fund recommendations remain unresolved potential compliance failures that could form the basis for a complaint under both the firm's internal process and through OBSI.

conversation.text: Marcus, I appreciate you meeting with me. My wife and I have about $1.2 million in our super and we're looking at retiring in three years. We want to make sure everything's in the right place.

conversation.speaker: advisor

This is in your best interest.

conversation.speaker: advisor
conversation.text: The MER is about 1.85 percent, which is competitive for actively managed funds. As for Pinnacle, yes, they're on our approved product list, and we do receive a platform rebate, but that doesn't influence my recommendation. I'm recommending it because it's the best option for you.

conversation.speaker: client
conversation.text: A platform rebate? How much is that? And shouldn't you have told me about that upfront before recommending it?

conversation.speaker: advisor

legal_assessment.analysis:
The adviser's conduct raises serious concerns across multiple international best interest frameworks. As the source document emphasizes, the best interest duty is not merely an obligation to act in a way the adviser 'honestly considered' to be in the client's interests — it is a 'positive obligation to act in what are, objectively, their interests.' Marcus's recommendation to concentrate 60% of a near-retiree's superannuation into a single managed fund with a 1.85% MER, where his firm receives a 40 basis point rebate, fails the objective standard. The recommendation appears to prioritize a conflicted product over genuine portfolio construction principles appropriate for the client's risk profile and time horizon. The adviser's dismissal of the client's legitimate questions about diversification and conflicts — characterizing them as 'fine print' — is particularly troubling.

Under Australian law (Corporations Act s961B), the adviser must demonstrate through a documented process that the recommendation is objectively in the client's best interest, having conducted reasonable inquiries and given appropriate consideration to the client's circumstances including proximity to retirement. The FASEA Code of Ethics (Standards 2, 3, and 5) reinforces that the adviser must not only avoid conflicts but must prioritize the client's interest where conflicts exist. Under MiFID II Article 25, a suitability assessment would require documented analysis showing why a concentrated position is appropriate for a risk-averse, pre-retirement client. The FCA Consumer Duty (PRIN 12) would scrutinize whether this product delivers fair value and a good outcome relative to the client's needs. IOSCO's 2021 Suitability Principles similarly require that conflicts be managed and disclosed proactively, not revealed only when the client probes.

The late and reluctant disclosure of the platform rebate, combined with the adviser's repeated use of the phrase 'best interest' without substantive justification, exemplifies the very confusion the source document identifies: the term is used 'glibly' while the adviser's process falls short of the objective, procedural standard the law demands. The recommendation lacks evidence of modern portfolio theory application, comparative product analysis, or genuine risk profiling aligned with the client's three-year retirement timeline.

Failure to conduct a proper suitability assessment considering the client's risk tolerance, investment horizon, and proximity to retirement (MiFID II Art. 25; ASIC s961B safe harbour steps)
Dismissal of client's legitimate concerns about diversification and conflicts, undermining informed consent and the duty to support good outcomes (FCA Consumer Duty PRIN 12.3)
Recommendation inconsistent with modern portfolio theory for a pre-retirement client, raising concerns about competency and process (IOSCO Suitability Principles 2021)
Use of the phrase 'best interest' as rhetorical reassurance rather than as a reflection of an objective, documented advisory process

legal_assessment.recommendation: The adviser should have conducted and documented a comprehensive fact-find and risk assessment before making any product recommendation, explicitly addressing the client's three-year retirement horizon and conservative risk appetite. All conflicts of interest, including the platform rebate, should have been disclosed proactively and in writing at the outset of the engagement — not revealed only when challenged. The recommendation should have been supported by comparative analysis of multiple suitable products, with documented reasoning for why the chosen product objectively serves the client's interests. A diversified, lower-cost portfolio strategy aligned with modern portfolio theory and the client's near-retirement status would have been far more defensible. The adviser should treat the best interest duty as a rigorous procedural and substantive obligation, not a rhetorical flourish.

conversation.text: Hi Marcus, thanks for seeing me. My wife and I have been talking about what to do with the proceeds from the sale of our rental property. It's about $620,000, and we're not sure where to put it.

conversation.speaker: client
conversation.text: What about the risk side of things though? My wife is quite conservative. She was actually asking whether you'd assess our risk tolerance properly — she read something about advisers needing to do that now under the new rules.

conversation.text: Look, we can go through a questionnaire if you like, but honestly, I've been doing this for twenty years. I can tell from our conversation that you're comfortable with a bit of risk if the returns are there. The questionnaire is more of a formality.

conversation.text: I suppose. But what about the bit for our daughter's fees? That's probably around $80,000 we'd need within twelve months.

conversation.speaker: advisor
conversation.text: We could put that in the same fund and just draw it down when you need it. The fund has monthly liquidity, so you can pull it out anytime.

conversation.speaker: client
conversation.text: A growth fund for money we need in twelve months? That doesn't sound right to me, Marcus. What if the market drops?

legal_assessment.analysis:
Marcus's conduct raises serious concerns under multiple regulatory frameworks. Under New Zealand's Financial Markets Conduct Act 2013 (as amended by the Financial Services Legislation Amendment Act 2019) and the new Code of Professional Conduct for Financial Advice Services, financial advisers owe a duty to give advice that is suitable for the client, taking into account the client's financial situation, goals, risk tolerance, and time horizon. Marcus dismissed the formal risk tolerance assessment as a 'formality,' when it is in fact a core regulatory requirement. His initial recommendation to place short-term funds (the $80,000 for university fees) into a growth fund demonstrated a fundamental suitability failure, though he corrected this when challenged. More concerning is his refusal to properly consider alternatives or document his reasoning, which breaches the requirement for a structured, repeatable, and defensible investment process — precisely the kind of governance framework the source document describes as essential.

The trust dimension compounds these issues significantly. Under New Zealand's Trusts Act 2019, trustees owe duties of care, honesty, good faith, and conflict avoidance. Marcus's dismissal of these obligations as his lawyer 'overthinking it' is both incorrect and potentially harmful. When advising on trust assets, the adviser must ensure the investment strategy is consistent with the trust deed, the trustees' duties, and the beneficiaries' interests. Internationally, this conduct would also fall short of the FCA Consumer Duty (PRIN 12) which requires firms to act to deliver good outcomes for retail customers, MiFID II Article 25 suitability requirements mandating a thorough assessment of client knowledge, experience, financial situation, and objectives, IOSCO's 2021 Suitability Principles requiring documented rationale and consideration of alternatives, and ASIC §961B's best interests duty requiring reasonable investigation of financial products.

Marcus's repeated reliance on personal judgment ('trust me'), his resistance to documenting recommendations, his failure to present alternatives, and his dismissive attitude toward the client's legitimate concerns about risk assessment and trustee obligations collectively paint a picture of an adviser prioritizing convenience and a favored product over genuine client-centered advice. The pattern of steering toward a single product without documented justification also raises potential conflict of interest questions — whether there are undisclosed commissions or volume-based incentives tied to the Kauri Growth Fund.
